entries.e81c419e283b94200ad35bcc53c83c19e8cffc62: <div sID="gen12944" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="122" osisID="Ps.122" sID="Ps.122"/> <div eID="gen12944" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12945" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen12946" type="x-p"/> This psalm seems to have been penned by David for the use of the people of Israel, when they came up to Jerusalem to worship at the three solemn feasts. It was in David's time that Jerusalem was first chosen to be the city where God would record his name. It being a new thing, this, among other means, was used to bring the people to be in love with Jerusalem, as the holy city, though it was but the other day in the hands of the Jebusites. Observe, I. The joy with which they were to go up to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Ps.122.1-Ps.122.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. The great esteem they were to have of Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Ps.122.3-Ps.122.5">ver. 3-5</reference>. III. The great concern they were to have for Jerusalem, and the prayers they were to put up for its welfare, <reference osisRef="Ps.122.6-Ps.122.9">ver. 6-9</reference>. In singing this psalm we must have an eye to the gospel church, which is called the "Jerusalem that is from above."
entries.2c4aee7fab2fa51927f99e9e2f9e41415b67f852: <div eID="gen12946" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen12945" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Pleasures of Public Worship.</title> <div sID="gen12947" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . <hi type="super">2</hi> Our feet shall stand within thy gates, O Jerusalem. <hi type="super">3</hi> Jerusalem is builded as a city that is compact together: <hi type="super">4</hi> Whither the tribes go up, the tribes of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , unto the testimony of Israel, to give thanks unto the name of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> . 5 For there are set thrones of judgment, the thrones of the house of David. <div eID="gen12947" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12948" type="x-p"/> Here we have, <div eID="gen12948" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12949" type="x-p"/> I. The pleasure which David and other pious Israelites took in approaching to and attending upon God in public ordinances, <reference osisRef="Ps.122.1-Ps.122.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. <div eID="gen12949" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12950" type="x-p"/> 1. The invitation to them was very welcome. David was himself glad, and would have every Israelite to say that he <hi type="italic">was glad, when</hi> he was called upon to <hi type="italic">go up to the house of the Lord.</hi> Note, (1.) It is the will of God that we should worship him in concert, that many should join together to wait upon him in public ordinances. We ought to worship God in our own houses, but that is not enough; we must <hi type="italic">go into the house of the Lord,</hi> to pay our homage to him there, and <hi type="italic">not forsake the assembling of ourselves together.</hi> (2.) We should not only agree with one another, but excite and stir up one another, to go to worship God in public. <hi type="italic">Let us go;</hi> not, "Do you go and pray for us, and we will stay at home;" but, <hi type="italic">We will go also,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.8.21">Zech. viii. 21</reference>. Not, "Do you go before, and we will follow at our leisure;" or, "We will go first, and you shall come after us;" but, "<hi type="italic">Let us go</hi> together, for the honour of God and for our mutual edification and encouragement." We ourselves are slow and backward, and others are so too, and therefore we should thus quicken and sharpen one another to that which is good, as iron sharpens iron. (3.) Those that rejoice in God will rejoice in calls and opportunities to wait upon him. David himself, though he had as little need of a spur to his zeal in religious exercises as any, yet was so far from taking it as an affront that he was glad of it as a kindness when he was called upon to <hi type="italic">go</hi> up <hi type="italic">to the house of the Lord</hi> with the meanest of his subjects. We should desire our Christian friends, when they have any good work in hand, to call for us and take us along with them. <div eID="gen12950" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12951" type="x-p"/> 2. The prospect of them was very pleasing. They speak it with a holy triumph (<reference osisRef="Ps.122.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">Our feet shall stand within thy gates, O Jerusalem!</hi> Those that came out of the country, when they found the journey tedious, comforted themselves with this, that they should be in Jerusalem shortly, and that would make amends for all the fatigues of their journey. We shall stand there as servants; it is desirable to have a place in Jerusalem, though it be <hi type="italic">among those that stand by</hi> (<reference osisRef="Zech.3.7">Zech. iii. 7</reference>), though it be the door keeper's place, <reference osisRef="Ps.84.10">Ps. lxxxiv. 10</reference>. We have now got a resting-place for the ark, and where it is there will we be. <div eID="gen12951" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12952" type="x-p"/> II. The praises of Jerusalem, as <reference osisRef="Ps.48.12">Ps. xlviii. 12</reference>. <div eID="gen12952" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12953" type="x-p"/> 1. It is the beautiful city, not only for situation, but for building. It is built into <hi type="italic">a city,</hi> the houses not scattered, but contiguous, and the streets fair and spacious. It is built uniform, <hi type="italic">compact together,</hi> the houses strengthening and supporting one another. Though the city was divided into the higher and lower town, yet the Jebusites being driven out, and it being entirely in the possession of God's people, it is said to be compact together. It was a type of the gospel-church, which is compact together in holy love and Christian communion, so that it is all as one city. <div eID="gen12953" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12954" type="x-p"/> 2. It is the holy city, <reference osisRef="Ps.122.4">v. 4</reference>. It is the place where all Israel meet one another: <hi type="italic">Thither the tribes go up,</hi> from all parts of the country, as one man, under the character of <hi type="italic">the tribes of the Lord,</hi> in obedience to his command. It is the place appointed for their general rendezvous; and they come together, (1.) To receive instruction from God; they come <hi type="italic">to the testimony of Israel,</hi> to hear what God has to say to them and to consult his oracle. (2.) To ascribe the glory to God, <hi type="italic">to give thanks to the name of the Lord,</hi> which we have all reason to do, especially those that have the testimony of Israel among them. If God speak to us by his word, we have reason to answer him by our thanksgivings. See on what errand we go to public worship, <hi type="italic">to give thanks.</hi> <div eID="gen12954" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12955" type="x-p"/> 3. It is the royal city (<reference osisRef="Ps.122.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">There are set thrones of judgment. Therefore</hi> the people had reason to be in love with Jerusalem, because justice was administered there by a man after God's own heart. The civil interests of the people were as well secured as their ecclesiastical concerns; and very happy they were in their courts of judicature, which were erected in Jerusalem, as with us in Westminster Hall. Observe, What a goodly sight it was to see <hi type="italic">the testimony of Israel</hi> and the <hi type="italic">thrones of judgment</hi> such near neighbours, and they are good neighbours, which may greatly befriend one another. Let the testimony of Israel direct the thrones of judgment, and the thrones of judgment protect the testimony of Israel.
entries.e50d51deb8e9100eef5cb9668c9636cf8bdb4439: <div eID="gen12955" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Prayer for the Church.</title> <div sID="gen12956" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: they shall prosper that love thee. <hi type="super">7</hi> Peace be within thy walls, <hi type="italic">and</hi> prosperity within thy palaces. <hi type="super">8</hi> For my brethren and companions' sakes, I will now say, Peace <hi type="italic">be</hi> within thee. 9 Because of the house of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God I will seek thy good. <div eID="gen12956" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12957" type="x-p"/> Here, I. David calls upon others to wish well to Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Ps.122.6-Ps.122.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. <hi type="italic">Pray for the peace of Jerusalem,</hi> for the welfare of it, for all good to it, particularly for the uniting of the inhabitants among themselves and their preservation from the incursions of enemies. This we may truly desire, that in the peace thereof we may have peace; and this we must earnestly pray for, for it is the gift of God, and for it he will be enquired of. Those that can do nothing else for the peace of Jerusalem can pray for it, which is something more than showing their good-will; it is the appointed way of fetching in mercy. The peace and welfare of the gospel church, particularly in our land, is to be earnestly desired and prayed for by every one of us. Now, 1. We are here encouraged in our prayers for Jerusalem's peace: <hi type="italic">Those shall prosper that love thee.</hi> We must pray for Jerusalem, not out of custom, nor for fashion's sake, but out of a principle of love to God's government of man and man's worship of God; and, in seeking the public welfare, we seek our own, for so well does God <hi type="italic">love the gates of Zion</hi> that he will love all those that do love them, and therefore they cannot but prosper; at least their souls shall prosper by the ordinances they so dearly love. 2. We are here directed in our prayers for it and words are put into our mouths (<reference osisRef="Ps.122.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">Peace be within thy walls.</hi> He teaches us to pray, (1.) For all the inhabitants in general, all within the walls, from the least to the greatest. Peace be in thy fortifications; let them never be attacked, or, if they be, let them never be taken, but be an effectual security to the city. (2.) For the princes and rulers especially: Let <hi type="italic">prosperity</hi> be <hi type="italic">in the palaces</hi> of the great men that sit at the helm and have the direction of public affairs; for, if they prosper, it will be well for the public. The poorer sort are apt to envy the prosperity of the palaces, but they are here taught to pray for it. <div eID="gen12957" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12958" type="x-p"/> II. He resolves that whatever others do he will approve himself a faithful friend to Jerusalem, 1. In his prayers: "<hi type="italic">I will now say,</hi> now I see the tribes so cheerfully resorting hither to <hi type="italic">the testimony of Israel,</hi> and the matter settled, that Jerusalem must be the place where God will record his name, now I will say, <hi type="italic">Peace be within thee.</hi>" He did not say, "Let others pray for the public peace, the priests and the prophets, whose business it is, and the people, that have nothing else to do, and I will fight for it and rule for it." No; "I will pray for it too." 2. In his endeavours, with which he will second his prayers: "<hi type="italic">I will,</hi> to the utmost of my power, <hi type="italic">seek thy good.</hi>" Whatever lies within the sphere of our activity to do for the public good we must do it, else we are not sincere in praying for it. Now it might be said, No thanks to David to be so solicitous for the welfare of Jerusalem; it was his own city, and the interests of his family were lodged in it. This is true; yet he professes that this was not the reason why he was in such care for the welfare of Jerusalem, but it proceeded from the warm regard he had, (1.) To the communion of saints: It is <hi type="italic">for my brethren and companions' sakes,</hi> that is, for the sake of all true-hearted Israelites, whom I look upon as my brethren (so he called them, <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.2">1 Chron. xxviii. 2</reference>) and who have often been my companions in the worship of God, which has knit my heart to them. (2.) To the ordinances of God: He had <hi type="italic">set his affections to the house of his God</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Chr.29.3">1 Chron. xxix. 3</reference>); he took a great pleasure in public worship, and for that reason would pray for the good of Jerusalem. <hi type="italic">Then</hi> our concern for the public welfare is right when it is the effect of a sincere love to God's institutions and his faithful worshippers.  <chapter eID="Ps.122"/> <div eID="gen12958" type="x-p"/>

entries.55045b555f5c3075be2d76e6fc004ccf0639d4fd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6991"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 122</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.122.1-Ps.122.9">Psa 122:1-9</reference>. This Psalm might well express the sacred joy of the pilgrims on entering the holy city, where praise, as the religious as well as civil metropolis, is celebrated, and for whose prosperity, as representing the Church, prayer is offered.</title> <div sID="gen10732" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6991"/><hi type="bold">1-2. Our feet shall stand--</hi>literally, "are standing." <div eID="gen10732" type="x-p"/>
entries.fba9dd5ae306ceca2764c8a80b7c179be34f5b1e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6993"/><div sID="gen10734" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6993"/><hi type="bold">3-5. compact together--</hi>all parts united, as in David's time. <div eID="gen10734" type="x-p"/>
entries.9974402e0e7ac3a09666e16ad3a76e6a86eedba6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6996"/><div sID="gen10737" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6996"/><hi type="bold">6-7. Let peace--</hi>including prosperity, everywhere prevail. <div eID="gen10737" type="x-p"/>
entries.a332b2c92b7f526eb4fb4ee8844d92f2129f4194: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6997"/><div sID="gen10738" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6997"/>8-9. In the welfare of the city, as its civil, and especially the religious relations, was involved that of Israel.<div eID="gen10738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10739" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">now--</hi>as in <reference osisRef="Ps.115.2">Psa 115:2</reference>. <div eID="gen10739" type="x-p"/>

entries.119ffbe44fd0299a41e7e9da8e78edd0581398db: <div eID="gen23017" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23018" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23019" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23019" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23018" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23020" type="x-p"/> The satisfaction of a gracious soul in the use of God's ordinances, <reference osisRef="Psa.122.1">Psa 122:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.122.2">Psa 122:2</reference>. Description of the internal governmentof Jerusalem, <reference osisRef="Psa.122.3-Psa.122.5">Psa 122:3-5</reference>. Prayers for its peace and prosperity, <reference osisRef="Psa.122.6-Psa.122.9">Psa 122:6-9</reference>. <div eID="gen23020" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23021" type="x-p"/> In the preceding Psalms we find the poor captives crying to God for deliverance; here they are returning thanks that they find they are permitted to return to their own land and to the ordinances of their God. <div eID="gen23021" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23022" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23022" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23023" type="x-p"/> I was glad when they said - When Cyrus published an edict for their return, the very first object of their thanksgiving was the kindness of God in permitting them to return to his ordinances.
entries.88573d8c3591bfa310423ca0df5aa49f792f9e17: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen23023" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23024" type="x-p"/> Our feet shad stand - For seventy years we have been exiled from our own land; our heart was in Jerusalem, but our feet were in Chaldea. Now God has turned our captivity, and our feet shall shortly stand within the gates of Jerusalem. What a transition from misery to happiness! and what a subject for rejoicing!
entries.ee0b4c2bc30dbbd674e9fc33913c98217c4a383c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23024" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23025" type="x-p"/> Jerusalem - compact together - It is now well rebuilt, every part contributing to the strength of the whole. It is also a state of great political and spiritual union. It is the center of union to all the tribes, for each tribe has an equal interest in that God who is worshipped there.
entries.0526ff8f42965eef900bf929383ac84d972e607c: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23025" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23026" type="x-p"/> The testimony of Israel - There is the ark, where the presence of God is manifested; there is the holy of holies; and there all the tribes assembled to worship Jehovah. He no doubt alludes to the assembling of the tribes annually at each of the three grand national festivals.
entries.fe4b66375c8b18974d001433e39052e2024da147: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23026" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23027" type="x-p"/> There are set thrones of judgment - There were the public courts, and thither the people went to obtain justice; and while the thrones of the house of David were there, they had justice.
entries.622f3575462b3f511326ac456871446597dfcc76: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23027" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23028" type="x-p"/> Pray for the peace of Jerusalem - שלום shalom signifies both peace and prosperity. Let her unanimity never be disturbed; let her prosperity ever be on the increase! <div eID="gen23028" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23029" type="x-p"/> They shall prosper that love thee - In the peace and prosperity of the city, they shall find their peace and their prosperity; and even on this ground they should love the city, and labor to promote its best interests. There is a remarkable alliteration in this verse, the letter ש shin frequently recurring. שאלו שלום ירושלם ישליו אהביך <div eID="gen23029" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23030" type="x-p"/> Shaalu shelom yerushalam yishlayu ohabeycha. "Ask ye the prosperity of Jerusalem; they shall be quiet that love thee." <div eID="gen23030" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23031" type="x-p"/> There are remarkable specimens of similar alliteration to be found in all poets, ancient and modern. This formed the chief feature of our ancient poetry. Thus in Peter the plouphman: - "In a somers seysoun whan sete was the sonne <div eID="gen23031" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23032" type="x-p"/> I schoop me in a shrowde as I a sheep were." <div eID="gen23032" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23033" type="x-p"/> And the same manner often appears, even in Milton himself. See the II Penseroso: - "Oft, on a plat of rising ground, <div eID="gen23033" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23034" type="x-p"/> I hear the far-off curfew sound <div eID="gen23034" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23035" type="x-p"/> Over some wide-watered shore, <div eID="gen23035" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23036" type="x-p"/> Swinging slow with sullen roar."
entries.6d42e0f2c0c1af601c5d893e48ed7f3606e23159: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23036" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23037" type="x-p"/> Peace be within thy walls - This is the form of prayer that they are to use: "May prosperity ever reside within thy walls, on all the people that dwell there; and tranquillity within thy palaces or high places, among the rulers and governors of the people."
entries.fb0f3665b43e2cced159ec77cc2cb4291ddf4dea: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen23037" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23038" type="x-p"/> For any brethren and companions' sakes - Because this city is the abode of my kinsfolk and countrymen, I will wish it prosperity. I will promote its peace and tranquillity by all means in my power. I will affectionately say, May peace be within thee!
entries.168ac25def53625e2872267653566874cd983fbb: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen23038" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23039" type="x-p"/> Because of the house of the Lord our God - Particularly will I wish thee well, because thou art the seat of religion, the place where our merciful God has condescended to dwell. <div eID="gen23039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23040" type="x-p"/> To the captives in Babylon the Prophet Jeremiah had given this charge, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.7">Jer 29:7</reference> : "And seek שלום shalom, the prosperity of the city, whither I have caused you to be carried captives, and pray unto the Lord for it; for in the prosperity thereof ye shall have prosperity." <div eID="gen23040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23041" type="x-p"/> Was this a duty for the captives? Yes. And is it the duty of every man for his own country! God, nature, common sense, and self-interest say, Yes! And what must we think of the wretches who not only do not thus pray, but labor to destroy the public peace, to subvert the government of their country, to raise seditions, and to destroy all its civil and religious institutions? Think of them! Why, that hemp would be disgraced by hanging them. <div eID="gen23041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23042" type="x-p"/> There is a fine picture given us here of the state of Jerusalem after the restoration of the Jews. The walls were finished, the city rebuilt, beautiful, strong, and regular, the temple and its worship were restored, the courts of justice were re-established, the constituted authorities in Church and state were doing their duty; and God was pouring out his blessing upon all. Who could see this without praying, May God increase thy peace, and establish thy prosperity for ever!  <chapter eID="Ps.122"/> <div eID="gen23042" type="x-p"/>

entries.ceebfa12e8cdc0fd95cf2865e1d0e838707d1d58: <div eID="gen10174" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">A Well-Wishing Glance Back at the Pilgrims’ City</title> <div sID="gen10175" type="x-p"/> If by “the mountains” in <reference osisRef="Ps.121.1">Psa 121:1</reference> the mountains of the Holy Land are to be understood, it is also clear for what reason the collector placed this Song of degrees, which begins with the expression of joy at the pilgrimage to the house of Jahve, and therefore to the holy mountain, immediately after the preceding song. By its peace-breathing (שׁלום) contents it also, however, touches closely upon <reference osisRef="Ps.120.1">Psa 120:1</reference>-7. The poet utters aloud his hearty benedictory salutation to the holy city in remembrance of the delightful time during which he sojourned there as a visitor at the feast, and enjoyed its inspiring aspect. If in respect of the לדוד the Psalm were to be regarded as an old Davidic Psalm, it would belong to the series of those Psalms of the time of the persecution by Absalom, which cast a yearning look back towards home, the house of God (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.1-Ps.23.6">Psa 23:1-6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.26.1-Ps.26.12">Psa 26:1-12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.55.15">Psa 55:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.61.1-Ps.61.8">Psa 61:1-8</reference>, and more particularly <reference osisRef="Ps.63.1-Ps.63.11">Psa 63:1-11</reference>). But the לדוד is wanting in the lxx, <hi type="italic">Codd. Alex.</hi> and <hi type="italic">Vat</hi>.; and the <hi type="italic">Cod Sinait.,</hi> which has ΤΩ ΔΑΔ, puts this before <reference osisRef="Ps.124.1-Ps.124.8">Psa 124:1-8</reference>, ει ̓ μὴ ὅτι κύριος κ. τ. λ., also, contrary to <hi type="italic">Codd. Alex.</hi> and <hi type="italic">Vat.</hi> Here it is occasioned by <reference osisRef="Ps.122.5">Psa 122:5</reference>, but without any critical discernment. The measures adopted by Jeroboam I show, moreover, that the pilgrimages to the feasts were customary even in the time of David and Solomon. The images of calves in Dan and Bethel, and the changing of the Feast of Tabernacles to another month, were intended to strengthen the political rupture, by breaking up the religious unity of the people and weaning them from visiting Jerusalem. The poet of the Psalm before us, however, lived much later. He lived, as is to be inferred with Hupfeld from <reference osisRef="Ps.122.3">Psa 122:3</reference>, in the time of the post-exilic Jerusalem which rose again out of its ruins. Thither he had been at one of the great feasts, and here, still quite full of the inspiring memory, he looks back towards the holy city; for, in spite of Reuss, Hupfeld, and Hitzig, Psa 122:1., so far as the style is concerned, are manifestly a retrospect.
entries.f7eac1d3e4b43f1b16dfdab3d86fa504232d38dd: <reference osisRef="Ps.122.1-Ps.122.3">Psa 122:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen10175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10176" type="x-p"/> The preterite שׂמחתי may signify: I rejoice (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.1">1Sa 2:1</reference>), just as much as: I rejoiced. Here in comparison with <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.122.2">Psa 122:2</reference></hi> it is a retrospect; for היה with the participle has for the most part a retrospective signification, <reference osisRef="Gen.39.22">Gen 39:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.9.22">Deu 9:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.9.24">Deu 9:24</reference>; Jdg 1:7; Job 1:14. True, עמדות היוּ might also signify: they have been standing and still stand (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.10.14">Psa 10:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.59.2">Isa 59:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.30.20">Isa 30:20</reference>); but then why was it not more briefly expressed by עמדוּ (<reference osisRef="Ps.26.12">Psa 26:12</reference>)? The lxx correctly renders: εὐφράνθην and ἑστῶτες ἦσαν. The poet, now again on the journey homewards, or having returned home, calls to mind the joy with which the cry for setting out, “Let us go up to the house of Jahve!” filled him. When he and the other visitors to the feast had reached the goal of their pilgrimage, their feet came to a stand-still, as if spell-bound by the overpowering, glorious sight.<note placement="foot">So also Veith in his, in many points, beautiful Lectures on twelve gradual Psalms (Vienna 1863), S. 72, “They arrested their steps, in order to give time to the amazement with which the sight of the Temple, the citadel of the king, and the magnificent city filled them.”</note> <div eID="gen10176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10177" type="x-p"/> Reviving this memory, he exclaims: Jerusalem, O thou who art built up again - true, בּנה in itself only signifies “to build,” but here, where, if there is nothing to the contrary, a closed sense is to be assumed for the line of the verse, and in the midst of songs which reflect the joy and sorrow of the post-exilic restoration period, it obtains the same meaning as in <reference osisRef="Ps.102.17">Psa 102:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.147.2">Psa 147:2</reference>, and frequently (Gesenius: <hi type="italic">O Hierosolyma restituta</hi>). The parallel member, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.122.3">Psa 122:3</reference></hi>, does not indeed require this sense, but is at least favourable to it. Luther’s earlier rendering, “as a city which is compacted together,” was happier than his later rendering, “a city where they shall come together,” which requires a <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. or <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. instead of the passive. חבּר signifies, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.28.7">Exo 28:7</reference>, to be joined together, to be united into a whole; and יחדּו strengthens the idea of that which is harmoniously, perfectly, and snugly closed up (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.133.1">Psa 133:1</reference>). The <hi type="italic">Kaph</hi> of כּעיר is the so-called <hi type="italic">Kaph veritatis</hi>: Jerusalem has risen again out of its ruined and razed condition, the breaches and gaps are done away with (<reference osisRef="Isa.58.12">Isa 58:12</reference>), it stands there as a closely compacted city, in which house joins on to house. Thus has the poet seen it, and the recollection fills him with rapture.<note placement="foot">In the synagogue and church it is become customary to interpret <reference osisRef="Ps.122.3">Psa 122:3</reference> of the parallelism of the heavenly and earthly Jerusalem.</note>
entries.239758820011841ff8e3232f3e70a79b7d7ef519: <reference osisRef="Ps.122.4-Ps.122.5">Psa 122:4-5</reference> <div eID="gen10177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10178" type="x-p"/> The imposing character of the impression was still greatly enhanced by the consideration, that this is the city where at all times the twelve tribes of God’s nation (which were still distinguished as its elements even after the Exile, <reference osisRef="Rom.11.1">Rom 11:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.2.36">Luk 2:36</reference>; Jam 1:1) came together at the three great feasts. The use of the שׁ twice as equivalent to אשׁר is (as in Canticles) appropriate to the ornamental, happy, miniature-like manner of these Songs of degrees. In שׁשּׁם the שׁם is, as in <reference osisRef="Eccl.1.7">Ecc 1:7</reference>, equivalent to שׁמּה, which on the other hand in <reference osisRef="Ps.122.5">Psa 122:5</reference> is no more than an emphatic שׁם (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.76.4">Psa 76:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.68.7">Psa 68:7</reference>). עלוּ affirms a habit (cf. <reference osisRef="Job.1.4">Job 1:4</reference>) of the past, which extends into the present. עדוּת לישׂראל is not an accusative of the definition or destination (Ew. §300, c), but an apposition to the previous clause, as e.g., in <reference osisRef="Lev.23.14">Lev 23:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.21">Lev 23:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.23.31">Lev 23:31</reference> (Hitzig), referring to the appointing in <reference osisRef="Exod.23.17">Exo 23:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.34.23">Exo 34:23</reference>; Deu 16:16. The custom, which arose thus, is confirmed in <reference osisRef="Ps.122.5">Psa 122:5</reference> from the fact, that Jerusalem, the city of the one national sanctuary, was at the same time the city of the Davidic kingship. The phrase ישׁב למשׁפּט is here transferred from the judicial persons (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.29.10">Psa 29:10</reference> with <reference osisRef="Ps.9.5">Psa 9:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.28.6">Psa 28:6</reference>), who sit in judgment, to the seats (thrones) which are set down and stand there fro judgment (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.125.1">Psa 125:1</reference>, and θρόνος ἔκειτο, <reference osisRef="Rev.4.2">Rev 4:2</reference>). The Targum is thinking of seats in the Temple, viz., the raised (in the second Temple resting upon pillars) seat of the king in the court of the Israelitish men near the שׁער העליון, but למשׁפט points to the palace, 1Ki 7:7. In the flourishing age of the Davidic kingship this was also the highest court of judgment of the land; the king was the chief judge (<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.2">2Sa 15:2</reference>; 1Ki 3:16), and the sons, brothers, or kinsmen of the king were his assessors and advisers. In the time of the poet it is different; but the attractiveness of Jerusalem, not only as the city of Jahve, but also as the city of David, remains the same for all times.
entries.5f53796ea5b9268785f23184d252834f5bcb5823: <reference osisRef="Ps.122.6-Ps.122.9">Psa 122:6-9</reference> <div eID="gen10178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10179" type="x-p"/> When the poet thus calls up the picture of his country’s “city of peace” before his mind, the picture of the glory which it still ever possesses, and of the greater glory which it had formerly, he spreads out his hands over it in the distance, blessing it in the kindling of his love, and calls upon all his fellow-countrymen round about and in all places: <hi type="italic">apprecamini salutem Hierosolymis</hi>. So Gesenius correctly (<hi type="italic">Thesaurus</hi>, p. 1347); for just as שׁאל לו לשׁלום signifies to inquire after any one’s well-being, and to greet him with the question: השׁלום לך (<reference osisRef="Jer.15.5">Jer 15:5</reference>), so שׁאל שׁלום signifies to find out any one’s prosperity by asking, to gladly know and gladly see that it is well with him, and therefore to be animated by the wish that he may prosper; Syriac, שׁאל שׁלמא ד directly: to salute any one; for the interrogatory השׁלום לך and the well-wishing שׁלום לך, εἰρήνη σοί (<reference osisRef="Luke.10.5">Luk 10:5</reference>; Joh 20:19.), have both of them the same source and meaning. The reading אהליך, commended by Ewald, is a recollection of <reference osisRef="Job.12.6">Job 12:6</reference> that is violently brought in here. The loving ones are comprehended with the beloved one, the children with the mother. שׁלה forms an alliteration with שׁלום; the emphatic form ישׁליוּ occurs even in other instances out of pause (e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.57.2">Psa 57:2</reference>). In <reference osisRef="Ps.122.7">Psa 122:7</reference> the alliteration of שׁלום and שׁלוה is again taken up, and both accord with the name of Jerusalem. <hi type="italic">Ad elegantiam facit</hi>, as Venema observes, <hi type="italic">perpetua vocum ad se invicem et omnium ad nomen Hierosolymae alliteratio</hi>. Both together mark the Song of degrees as such. Happiness, cries out the poet to the holy city from afar, be within thy bulwarks, prosperity within thy palaces, i.e., without and within. חיל, ramparts, circumvallation (from חוּל, to surround, Arabic <hi type="italic">hawl</hi>, round about, equally correct whether written חיל or חל), and ארמנות as the parallel word, as in Psa 48:14. The twofold motive of such an earnest wish for peace is love for the brethren and love for the house of God. For the sake of the brethren is he cheerfully resolved to speak peace (τὰ πρὸς ἐιρήνην αὐτῆς, <reference osisRef="Luke.19.42">Luk 19:42</reference>) concerning (דּבּר בּ, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.87.3">Psa 87:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.6.7">Deu 6:7</reference>, lxx περὶ σοῦ; cf. דּבּר שׁלום with אל and ל, to speak peace to, <reference osisRef="Ps.85.9">Psa 85:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Esth.10.3">Est 10:3</reference>) Jerusalem, for the sake of the house of Jahve will he strive after good (i.e., that which tends to her well-being) to her (like בּקּשׁ טובה ל in <reference osisRef="Neh.2.10">Neh 2:10</reference>, cf. דּרשׁ שׁלום, <reference osisRef="Deut.23.6">Deu 23:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.29.7">Jer 29:7</reference>). For although he is now again far from Jerusalem after the visit that is over, he still remains united in love to the holy city as being the goal of his longing, and to those who dwell there as being his brethren and friends. Jerusalem is and will remain the heart of all Israel as surely as Jahve who has His house there, is the God of all Israel.  <chapter eID="Ps.122"/> <div eID="gen10179" type="x-p"/>

entries.8dbcb0d501de584a2dcfebc41dbae01f872bfae9:
PSALM 122
In this Psalm David congratulates himself and the whole Church upon the fact, that a seat had at length been appointed for the ark of the covenant, and that God had chosen a place where his name should be continually called upon. Afterwards, to incite and encourage the faithful to engage in the worship of the sanctuary, he briefly declares, that the prosperous condition of the people depended upon God’s having chosen the seat of royalty to be at Jerusalem, from whence it was his purpose to defend, maintain, and assist his people.
A Song of Degrees of David.
“The burden of the Psalm,” says Jebb, “is שלום ‘peace.’ The play upon the words is very remarkable: שם, ‘there,’ and שם, ‘the name,’ lines 5 and 6; שבטים, ‘tribes,’ line 5 משפט, line 7. Then in line 9, and those. which follow: שאלו, ‘pray;’ שלום, ‘peace;’ ירושלם, ‘Jerusalem;’ ישליו, ‘shall prosper;’ שלוה ‘prosperity.’” — Jebb’s Literal Translation of the Psalters, with Dissertations, volume 1. Speaking in reference to the author of the Psalm, and to the opinion held by some critics, that it was composed about the time or’ the restoration of the Jews from Babylon, he says —”The extraordinary play upon words already noticed might argue a later period of composition: [than the time of David]. Still I cannot but think that the title assigning the Psalm to him is borne out by internal evidence of a stronger kind. The fond mention of Jerusalem, David’s beloved city; the thrones of the house of David; and the recurrence of peace, which was so emphatically promised to David, as the blessing about to be conferred on his son Solomon, are all circumstances, which, taken in connection, stamp this song with a character evidently belonging to the reign of the royal Psalmist ” — Ibid., volume 2.
Psalm 122:1-3
1. I was glad when they said to me, We will go into the house of Jehovah. 2. Our feet shall be
“Ou, ont este. — Fr. marg. “Or, have been.”
standing within thy gates, O Jerusalem! 3. Jerusalem is built as a city, compact in itself together.
Literally, Jerusalem built as a city, that is joined to itself together’, i.e. the several parts of which are connected with each other, so as to form one compact whole. Before David’s time, Zion was not a part of Jerusalem, neither it seems was Millo: but he added them to the city, and enclosed them within its wall. (2 Samuel 5:7, 9; 1 Chronicles 11:7, 8.) Solomon afterwards added the hill of Moria, on which his temple was built, to Jerusalem.” — Cresswell.
 
1 I was glad when they said to me. God had often told Moses, that his Sanctuary would one day have a certain and fixed place of abode; yet from the time of Moses, for the space of more than a thousand years, the Ark of the Covenant had been carried about from place to place, as if it had been in a state of pilgrimage. At length it was revealed to David, that mount Zion was the spot where God would have his ark to be settled, and his temple built. Now, as David himself received this revelation with exceeding great joy, so he affirms that he was glad to find the whole people with one consent agreeing thereto. This circumstance has not been duly considered, and the consequence is, that interpreters have given the unhappy translation—I was glad with those that said to me. Such a rendering, however, only renders the sense a little obscure; but the translation of the Septuagint and the Vulgate, which puts upon the second verb of the verse a neuter signification, entirely vitiates the meaning, I was glad in the things which, were said to me. I indeed admit that literally the reading is—I was glad in those who said to me; but it is no uncommon thing for the letter ב, beth, which commonly signifies in, to be resolved into the adverb of time when; and here the scope of the text requires such a rendering. David testifies that he felt in his heart a double joy on observing that the whole people concurred in yielding obedience to the oracle which declared mount Zion to be the place which God had chosen for his solemn worship. By this example we are taught, that our joy, in like manner, should be doubled, when God by his Holy Spirit not only frames each of us to the obedience of his word, but also produces the same effect upon others, that we may be united together in the same faith. So stubborn and rebellious is human nature, that the great majority of mankind invariably murmur against God whenever he speaks. We have, therefore, no small ground for rejoicing when all harmoniously rank themselves with us on the side of God. Such as translate, with those who said to me, deduce this meaning: I take delight in the company of those who allure me to the service of God, and offer themselves to me as companions, that we may go to the sanctuary together. But from the second verse it will be still more obvious, that the joy of which David speaks proceeded from his seeing the people, with the ready obedience of faith, giving their consent to the utterance of the heavenly oracle, respecting the spot chosen to be the lawful and permanent scat of the ark of the covenant. For it immediately follows —

                  <ns0:head>PSAL. CXXII.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:head>A song of degrees of David.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:argument>
                     <ns0:p>This Psalm seems to have been written by <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> for the use of the people when they came up to <ns0:hi>Ierusalem</ns0:hi> to the so<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lemn Feasts.</ns0:p>
                  </ns0:argument>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1 I Was glad when they said unto me, Let us go <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Exhorting one another to it, as <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 33. 19. Or, <ns0:hi>we will go.</ns0:hi> The sence is, It delighted me much to hear that the people, who had so long lived in the neglect or contempt of Gods worship, were now ready and forward in it.</ns0:note> into the house of the LORD.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 Our feet <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>were standing.</ns0:hi> So Gr.</ns0:note> shall stand <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Thither we shall come, and there we shall make our abode during the times of solemn worship.</ns0:note> within thy gates, O Jerusalem <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">In that City, where the Ark is now fixed. We shall wander no more from place to place as the Ark was removed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:509" />3 Jerusalem is built as a city, that is <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">See 2 Sam. 5. 9.</ns0:note> com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pact together <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">Partly in its buildings, which are not dispersed, as they are in Villages, nor divided into two Cities, as it was before, but united and enlarged, 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 11. 7, 8. and principally in its Government and Religion, which was distinct and op<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />posite before <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> took the Fort of <ns0:hi>Zion</ns0:hi> from the <ns0:hi>Iebusites.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Exod. 23. 17. Deut. 16. 16.</ns0:note> Whither the tribes <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Not some few pious people of each Tribe, as in <ns0:hi>Sauls</ns0:hi> time and under the Judges, but whole Tribes, nor onely one or two of the Tribes, as it was during the late Civil Wars, but all the twelve Tribes.</ns0:note> go up, the tribes of the LORD <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">Whom God hath chosen to be his people, and whom he hath invited and required to resort thither.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>unto</ns0:hi> the testimony of Israel <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">Unto the Ark, which is oft called <ns0:hi>the Testimony,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 16. 34. <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 16. 13. & 24. 3. <ns0:hi>Numb.</ns0:hi> 17. 4. and more fully <ns0:hi>the Ark of the Testimony,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 26. 33, 34. and elsewhere, because of the Tables of the Covenant laid up in it, which are called Gods <ns0:hi>Testimony,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>the Tables of the Te<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stimony,</ns0:hi> as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 25. 16. & 31. 18, &c. And this may well be called <ns0:hi>the Testimony of</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>to Israel,</ns0:hi> because it was given by God to them and for their good. Or, by or according <ns0:hi>to the Testimony of Israel, i. e.</ns0:hi> Gods command given to <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> which may be alledged here as the reason which moved them to this journey.</ns0:note>, to give thanks unto the name of the LORD <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">To worship God, this one eminent part and action thereof being put for all the rest.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">5 For <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">This is added as another reason inviting and obliging them to go up to <ns0:hi>Ierusalem,</ns0:hi> and as another commendation of this City.</ns0:note> there <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> Do sit.</ns0:note> are set thrones of judgment <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">The supreme Courts of Justice for Ecclesia<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stical, and especially for Civil affairs, as the next clause ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />plains it.</ns0:note>: the thrones of the house of David <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The Royal Throne allotted by God to <ns0:hi>David</ns0:hi> and to his posterity for ever, and the inferior Seats of Justice established by and under his Authority. See 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 19. 8, 9, 10.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 Pray for the peace of Jerusalem <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">In whose prosperity both your Civil and your Religious priviledges are deeply concerned.</ns0:note>: they shall prosper <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>let them prosper,</ns0:hi> the future being taken imperatively, as is very frequent. The Lord grant them prosperity and all happiness.</ns0:note> that love it.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7 Peace be within thy walls <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">In all thy dwellings.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> prosperity within thy palaces <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Especially in the Court and the dwellings of the Princes and Rulers, whose welfare is a pub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lick blessing to all the people.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 For my brethren and companions sakes <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">And this I desire not onely nor chiefly for my own secu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rity and for the glory of mine Empire, but for the sake of all my fellow-citizens and of all the Israelites, whom, though my Subjects, I must owne for my brethren and companions in the chief priviledges and blessings enjoyed at <ns0:hi>Ierusalem.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, I will now say, Peace <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> within thee.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9 Because of the house of the LORD our God <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Which is now fixed in this City.</ns0:note>, I will <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Neh. 2. 10.</ns0:note> seek thy good.</ns0:p>
